overview: This 502-page file documents the U.S. Occupation’s investigation and restructuring of Japanese education in the immediate postwar period. Its SCAP Civil Information and Education Section reports cover the demilitarization and democratization of physical education, the history and postwar circumstances of foreign students—especially Chinese and former colonial students—Korean-language schools, and educational institutions affiliated with Christian, Buddhist, and Shinto organizations. Most of the file consists of detailed statistical censuses and institutional rosters for Miyazaki, Fukui, and Fukushima prefectures, recording schools’ administrative control, level, location, founding date, enrollment, and staffing, principally as of April and November 1946. Transmitting despatches, maps, an archival charge-out form, and a critical handwritten comment on a SCAP anniversary statement supplement the formal reports.
interest: The file is especially useful because it combines policy-oriented studies of educational democratization with unusually granular evidence about Japan’s school system immediately after the war. The prefectural rosters permit local and comparative research into enrollment, staffing, gender, school type, administrative jurisdiction, and the survival or reorganization of prewar institutions. Reports on foreign, colonial, and Korean students illuminate how education intersected with Japanese imperial legacies and postwar minority politics, while the survey of religious schools reveals the institutional geography of Christianity, Buddhism, and Shinto. The handwritten dismissal of a SCAP anniversary statement also provides a rare informal counterpoint to the file’s otherwise bureaucratic Occupation language.
